session.reading_goal: Explore potential use in my research
session.research_context: I am a PhD student in NLP moving into HCI. My project studies how non-expert users write prompts for LLM-based tools, and I plan to run a user study.

messages.text: Hi, I am reading this paper for my project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM tools. Could you tell me what the main findings of the paper are? I want to know if they are useful for me.

messages.short_answer: The main findings are that non-AI experts explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming and interactive machine learning, with human-to-human instruction expectations and overgeneralization acting as barriers. These findings look relevant to your user study, though the sample was small and non-representative.

sections.title: Core findings reported in the abstract
sections.text: The authors report that probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and that expectations from human-to-human instruction and a tendency to overgeneralize were barriers to effective prompt design. The paper also describes participants who declared success after a single successful instance and rarely used error labeling or systematic testing.

sections.title: Further findings on mismatched expectations
sections.text: According to the overview of the appendix-level findings, participants expected plain behavioral descriptions to be understood and semantically equivalent prompts to give equivalent results, but trivial prompt changes often produced large output shifts. Participants also favored direct instructions over examples and often used 'do not' phrasing, even though 'do' phrasing was more effective.

sections.title: Why this may matter for your user study
sections.text: Your study of how non-experts write prompts for LLM tools could use these findings as hypotheses to probe, such as whether participants stop after one success or prefer instructions over examples. The paper's think-aloud and observation approach with a design probe may also be a useful method reference.

sections.title: Limits of these findings
sections.text: The paper states that the participant pool skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative, and that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants. The authors also list a small early-adopter academic sample and generalization to other populations and non-chatbot domains as open questions.

sources.text: Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts J.D. Zamfrescu-Pereira zamf@berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA Bjoern Hartmann bjoern@eecs.berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA ABSTRACT Pre-trained large language models (“LLMs”) like GPT-3 can engage in fuent, multi-turn instruction-taking out-of-the-box, making them attractive materials for designing natural language interactions. Using natural language to steer LLM outputs (“prompting”) has emerged as an important design technique potentially accessible to non-AI-experts. Crafting efective prompts can be challenging, however, and prompt-based interactions are brittle. Here, we explore whether non-AI-experts can successfully engage in “end-user prompt engineering” using a design probe—a prototype LLM-based chatbot design tool supporting development and systematic evaluation of prompting strategies. Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems.

sources.text: These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages describe a seven-step iterative prompt design workflow used with the BotDesigner tool, in which a user identifies and labels errors in chatbot conversations, debugs them by editing the prompt, and evaluates fixes locally and globally, framed as a regression-test approach that extends prior ad-hoc prompt tools. They then outline a user study with 10 non-expert prompt designers who had little prompt design experience, using think-aloud while improving a baseline chatbot. The study task asked participants to make a cooking chatbot resemble a professional chef from the web series Back to Back Chef, a task chosen over open-ended chatbot creation because pilot users mostly explored capabilities rather than iterating on prompts. The authors note the participant pool is skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative, so they make no claims about general population prevalence. They also note that the sample size follows prior formative usability work aimed at easy-to-find problems.

These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

messages.text: Okay, I think I understand the setup now. So the participants in this study are basically like the test set for evaluating the LLM tool, right? Like they are the held-out data that shows how well the prompts work for real users?

messages.short_answer: Not quite. In this paper the participants are not held-out test data for measuring how well the LLM tool's prompts perform. They are non-AI-expert end users who tried to design prompts with a prototype tool (BotDesigner, a design probe), and the researchers observed and interviewed them about how they approached and struggled with that design work.

sections.title: What participants did in the study
sections.text: The authors developed a no-code prompt design tool, BotDesigner, as a design probe and ran a user study with components of contextual inquiry and interview. Participants were asked to think aloud while the researchers analysed what prompt design approaches they tried and where they struggled.

sections.title: Why participants are not a test set
sections.text: A held-out test set is data used to measure a model's accuracy or output quality. Here, the study measured how people behave when they write prompts: their strategies, their intuitions, and their breakdowns. The participants' prompting behaviour is the object of study, not a benchmark for the tool's outputs.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: For your project on how non-experts write prompts, the participants would be your study subjects whose behaviour and reasoning you analyse, rather than evaluation data for the LLM. You would need to decide what you measure, such as strategies, expectations, or outcomes, and how you will record them, for example with think-aloud protocols as in this paper. This is a suggestion for you to weigh against your own design.

sections.title: Limits of this sample
sections.text: The authors state that their participant pool is not representative of the population at large, and the sample was small. Their stated goal was to find the first, easy-to-find problems users encounter, so the study is formative rather than a basis for generalising about all non-experts.

messages.text: Ok, so the participants are the subjects, not the test set. Got it. Then what is the probe? Is it like a baseline model you compare against?

messages.short_answer: No. In this paper, the design probe is BotDesigner, a no-code prototype prompt-design tool that the authors built and gave to participants so they could observe how non-experts approach prompt design. It is not a baseline model that the study compares against, and the retrieved passages do not describe any such comparison.

sections.title: What BotDesigner is in this study
sections.text: The authors say they developed a no-code prompt design tool, BotDesigner, as a design probe and ran a user study with contextual inquiry and interview components. They then observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience built a chatbot with it.

sections.title: Why a probe rather than a baseline
sections.text: A design probe is used to provoke and observe behaviour, not to measure the performance of a reference system. The authors argue that hands-on design work reveals more than interviews about hypothetical scenarios, so the tool serves as a way to see how people think and act. Their stated goals were to let end-users create chatbots without code and evaluate their prompts, while observing their intuitive behaviour.

sections.title: What this could mean for your user study
sections.text: If you run a user study, a probe-style tool could be one way to elicit how non-experts write and debug prompts, rather than only asking them about it. The paper also presents BotDesigner as a contribution in itself, so you would need to decide whether you build a probe or use an existing tool, and justify that choice in your own design. This is a possible use you may want to weigh, not a conclusion the paper draws for your project.

sources.text: Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

persona_text:
# Persona: Kenji

**Who.** Kenji is a Japanese PhD student in natural language processing (field A) who wants to move into
human-computer interaction (field B) and run user studies, but knows little HCI methodology. He writes
fluent but imperfect English and occasionally asks for a key term to be explained in Japanese.

**What he wants.** To learn how HCI studies people and to judge which of its methods he could borrow for his
project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM-based tools. Reading goal: *Explore potential use in my
research*.

**How he behaves.**
- Writes in English with small grammar mistakes. Interface language: English.
- Is precise about NLP terms but maps HCI concepts onto NLP ones ("so the participants are like the test
  set?", "is the design probe a kind of baseline model?"). Some of these analogies are wrong.
- Changes focus mid-conversation, e.g. from the findings to how the study was run.
- Asks about the strength of the evidence (number of participants, how the data were coded or analysed).
- Checks the sources often.
- Asks for a critical review of whether a method fits his project; his own verdict sometimes differs from
  PaperLens's suggestion.

**Paper.** Why Johnny Can't Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts.
